BINBETA and MULTIBIN: blinded binomial models

Source: vignettes/binbeta.Rmd
binbeta.Rmd
library(bssd)

One study: Ball and Schnell (2016)

With \(N\) enrolled subjects of whom \(Z\) had the event, the number on control is \(M_c \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N, 1 / (k + 1))\), the numbers with the event are \(Y_c \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(M_c, \theta_c)\) and \(Y_d \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N - M_c, \theta_d)\), \(Z = Y_c + Y_d\), and the proportions have Beta priors. Summing over \(M_c\) gives \(Z \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N, (\theta_c + k \theta_d) / (k + 1))\), so the posterior of \((\theta_c, \theta_d)\) is two-dimensional. binbeta_post() integrates it numerically; Ball and Schnell (2016) raise a signal when the posterior probability that \(\theta_d\) exceeds the maximum acceptable proportion is larger than a threshold.

fit <- binbeta_post(y = 40, n = 300, k = 1, prior_c = c(31, 271),
                    prior_d = c(1, 1), p0 = 0.15, cutoff = 0.8)
fit
#> Model: BINBETA 
#> Tested quantity: proportion theta_d of study drug
#> P(theta_d > 0.15 | data) = 0.6615
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.8): no
#> Posterior of rr: mean 1.724, median 1.652, 95% interval (0.7135, 3.151)
#> Posterior of theta_d: mean 0.1689, median 0.1677, 95% interval (0.08793, 0.2566)

Before the trial, the largest acceptable number of subjects with the event can be computed for each number of enrolled subjects (Figure 1 of Ball and Schnell, 2016); signal_count() returns the smallest number with a signal, which is one more than the largest acceptable number.

signal_count(n = c(50, 100, 200, 300), method = "binbeta",
             prior_c = c(31, 271), prior_d = c(1, 1), p0 = 0.15,
             cutoff = 0.8)
#>     n y_crit      prob prob_below
#> 1  50      8 0.8091985  0.6895111
#> 2 100     16 0.8599635  0.7912753
#> 3 200     30 0.8455281  0.7965627
#> 4 300     43 0.8087599  0.7649654

The binomial expansion of the likelihood makes the posterior a finite mixture of products of Beta distributions, which gives exact values. The largest absolute difference of the 21 compared quantities from these exact values (inst/validation/validate_methods_python.R, relative tolerance 1e-5) is 8.7e-07.

Several studies: Goren et al. (2020)

For several blinded studies, Goren et al. (2020) assume \(Y_s \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N_s, \theta_s (1 - r_s + r_s \delta))\) with study-specific control probabilities \(\theta_s \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a_s, b_s)\), a common rate ratio with \(\log \delta \sim N(m, v^2)\), and \(\theta_s \le 1 / \delta\). Given \(\delta\), each \(\theta_s\) is integrated out separately, so the posterior of \(\delta\) is one-dimensional and multibin_post() integrates it without MCMC.

The real data of Goren et al. (2020, Table 3) are eight studies; the homogeneous control prior is from 20 events among 1687 control patients of a previous trial.

y <- c(8, 4, 5, 6, 20, 2, 7, 39)
n <- c(354, 305, 307, 582, 244, 68, 307, 1612)
k <- c(2, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1)
fit <- multibin_post(y, n, k = k, prior_c = c(20, 1667), rr0 = 2)
fit
#> Model: MULTIBIN 
#> Tested quantity: rate ratio delta common to the studies
#> P(delta > 2 | data) = 0.9828
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): yes
#> Posterior of delta: mean NA, median 2.951, 95% interval (2.061, 4.093)

inst/reproduce/reproduce_Goren2020.R compares the posterior probabilities of Table 4 (homogeneous and heterogeneous priors, all studies and without study 5), which the authors computed by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo:

quantity published bssd tolerance judgement
P(delta > 1), full analysis, homogeneous priors 1.000 1.000 0.0020 PASS
P(delta > 2), full analysis, homogeneous priors 0.984 0.983 0.0035 PASS
P(delta > 3), full analysis, homogeneous priors 0.462 0.462 0.0125 PASS
P(delta > 1), full analysis, heterogeneous priors 1.000 1.000 0.0020 PASS
P(delta > 2), full analysis, heterogeneous priors 0.836 0.839 0.0095 PASS
P(delta > 3), full analysis, heterogeneous priors 0.158 0.158 0.0095 PASS
P(delta > 1), sensitivity analysis, homogeneous priors 0.998 0.998 0.0020 PASS
P(delta > 2), sensitivity analysis, homogeneous priors 0.561 0.563 0.0125 PASS
P(delta > 3), sensitivity analysis, homogeneous priors 0.034 0.035 0.0035 PASS
P(delta > 1), sensitivity analysis, heterogeneous priors 0.994 0.995 0.0035 PASS
P(delta > 2), sensitivity analysis, heterogeneous priors 0.486 0.485 0.0125 PASS
P(delta > 3), sensitivity analysis, heterogeneous priors 0.031 0.031 0.0035 PASS

The simulation of Table 2 (inst/reproduce/reproduce_Goren2020_simulation.R) has not been run for this installation.

Against nested adaptive quadrature in Python, the largest absolute difference of the 10 compared quantities is 3.7e-07.

Comparison with MCMC

model quantity MCMC bssd judgement
BINBETA P(theta_d > 0.15 | data) 0.6608 0.6615 PASS
BINBETA P(rr > 1 | data) 0.8965 0.8969 PASS
BINBETA MCMC proportion below the bssd posterior median 0.5000 0.5015 PASS
MULTIBIN P(delta > 1 | data) 0.7656 0.7692 PASS
MULTIBIN posterior mean of log(delta) 0.3546 0.3694 PASS
MULTIBIN MCMC proportion below the bssd posterior median 0.5000 0.4994 PASS

The JAGS models are in inst/validation/validate_jags_methods.R; for BINBETA, the number on control and the numbers with the event in each arm are latent variables.
